chapters.title: TISAX Audit Practice (1) — Preparation and Planning
chapters.title_en: TISAX Audit Practice (1): Preparation and Planning
intro: In the previous chapters we read the ISA control by control. This chapter turns the controls into a project you can actually run: from gap analysis, through scope definition, risk assessment, writing documents, implementation, internal audit, management review and the ISA self-assessment, all the way to the formal assessment.

We also provide a document list mapped to ISA controls, a RACI table for roles and responsibilities, and good and bad examples of the "Implementation description" and "Reference documentation" fields in the ISA self-assessment, so you can take them straight back to your company and use them.

blocks.text: 1. Implementation roadmap

head: Phase
Main activities
Main outputs
Related ISA controls
rows: 1. Gap analysis

Go through the original ISA 2027.1 text question by question in interviews, review evidence, and record the current maturity level and gaps. Also confirm the assessment objectives the customer requires.
Gap analysis report, list of improvement projects
All
2. Define the scope
Decide the TISAX assessment scope (sites, organization, processes), confirm the assessment objectives and assessment level, and register with ENX.
ISMS scope document, ENX registration data
3. Risk assessment
Build the asset inventory and classification, identify risks, assign risk owners and set up treatment plans.
Asset inventory, risk register, treatment plan
4. Write documents
Write policies, procedures and forms based on the gaps, and set up document control.
Policies, procedures and forms, document control list
5. Implementation
Put technical and organizational measures in place (MFA, EDR, backup, access control, training) and start building up records.
System configurations, records, training records
Chapters 2–9
6. Internal audit
Audit question by question against the ISA, record non-conformities and track corrections.
Internal audit plan, report, corrective action tracking
7. Management review
Management reviews ISMS effectiveness, risks, audit results and resources.
Management review records
8. ISA self-assessment
Fill in maturity levels, implementation descriptions and reference documentation in the latest ISA version and submit it to the audit provider.
ISA self-assessment
All
9. Formal assessment
Document review, interviews and on-site inspection according to AL2 or AL3, followed by handling of findings and the CAP.
Assessment report, CAP, label
All

blocks.text: 2. Typical timelines (for reference only)
Real timelines vary widely with company size, existing foundation, assessment objectives and resources. The ranges below are common in consulting practice and are **not ENX rules**:

head: Situation
Typical total duration
Notes
rows: ISO 27001 already in place and running for more than one year
About 3–6 months
Mainly add ISA-specific requirements, high protection needs requirements and evidence for maturity level 3.
Basic IT management, but no ISMS
About 6–12 months
A complete ISMS framework must be built, and processes must run for some time to build up records.
Prototype Protection added (AL3)
Add about 2–6 months
Physical improvements (fences, access control, intrusion detection, visual screening) often need construction and purchasing time.
Multiple sites or SGA
Depends on the number of sites and degree of centralization
First confirm the centralized processes and consistency across sites, then plan sampling and the assessment sequence.

blocks.title: Maturity level 3 needs "time"
blocks.text: Maturity level 3 requires "evidence that the process has been used continuously and actively over a longer period of time". A process that was released last week and has only one record is hard to rate as 3. In practice, let a new process run through at least one full cycle (for example one quarter of account reviews, one restore test, one internal audit and one management review) before the assessment.

What I fear most is a client saying: "The assessment is next month, so we will finish writing the documents this month." Finished documents are only the start of maturity level 2. What really takes time is getting the processes running and producing records.
3. Document list (policies, procedures and records mapped to ISA controls)

Use the table below as a document inventory checklist. You can rename or merge documents to fit your company. The key point is that for every control you can find the matching rule and the records showing it is in operation.

Type
ISA controls
Key content

Approved by management; includes information security objectives and significance; published on the intranet; relevant changes communicated to employees and external partners.

Defines the ISMS scope, the organization's requirements for the ISMS and the applicable controls; consistent with the TISAX scope.

Procedure / Record

Procedure / Record

Procedure / Record

Procedure / Record
Requirement specifications, secure configuration, acceptance before go-live, handling of test data.

Procedure / Record
Supplier risk assessment, security clauses in contracts, passing requirements down the supply chain, evidence (high protection needs).

NDA signed before sensitive information is disclosed, template reviewed by legal, validity monitored.
Responsibility matrix for external IT services
Record
List of IT services, responsible party for each security requirement, shared responsibility mechanisms, proof of fulfillment.
List of legal and contractual requirements (incl. data protection law such as the GDPR, customer requirements)
Record

Prototype protection policy and list of customer project requirements
Policy / Record

Record
Documentation of prototypes with traceable changes, proof of disposal according to customer rules.
Data protection policy, records of processing activities and personal data incident procedure
Policy / Record
Policy for processing personal data on behalf of others, inventory of processing activities, data transfers, data subject requests, data protection incidents, processing according to instructions.

blocks.text: Taking notes! You do not need many documents, but they must be "easy to find, the latest version, approved by someone, and backed by records that prove they are really used".

blocks.text: The most common RACI problem is "IT is A for everything". Information security is not just an IT topic: personnel screening belongs to HR, access control to facilities, suppliers to purchasing, and prototypes to R&D and facilities. In interviews, the auditor will go straight to these departments.
5. ISA self-assessment: how to write the Implementation description and Reference documentation

items: **Implementation description**: describe "who does what, with which tool, how often, and which records are kept", and respond to each Must, Should and applicable high / very high requirement.
**Should requirements not implemented**: state the reason, the impact assessment and who approved it. Do not leave it blank.
**The following aspects are considered**: write down your decision and the reason for each aspect.
**Reference documentation**: give the document number, title, version and record names so the auditor can request them directly. Avoid writing only "see ISMS documents".

**Maturity level**: be honest. Rating yourself too high makes the auditor lose trust in the whole self-assessment; if you rate yourself low but the evidence is strong, the auditor will usually rate based on the evidence.

**Language**: the self-assessment can be written in English or in a language accepted by the audit provider. Consider bilingual document titles (local language and English) so that foreign auditors can understand them easily.

head: Control
Weak answer
Good answer (Implementation description)
Reference documentation
rows: 1.1.1 Information security policy
We have a security policy and all employees know it.

The "Information Security Policy" v3.0 was approved by the managing director on 2026-03-15. It includes security objectives and sanctions for policy violations. It is published in the "ISMS area" of the intranet, and new employees sign it on their first day. The policy is reviewed every year in the management review; the changes in the 2026 version were sent by e-mail to all employees and to the 3 on-site contractors.
ISMS-P-001 Information Security Policy v3.0; management review record 2026-03; screenshot of announcement e-mail; new employee acknowledgement records
4.1.3 User account management
IT manages accounts and deletes them when people leave.

Account requests, changes and deactivation are handled through ITSM tickets according to the "Account and Access Management Procedure". Submitting the HR leaver form creates a ticket on the same day, and IT disables the AD and M365 accounts before the end of the last working day. Shared accounts are limited to 2 production HMI workstations, approved by the information security officer and recorded in the exception list. Account reviews are performed every six months, including customer portal accounts.
ISMS-I-004 Account and Access Management Procedure; account review report H1 2026; sample of leaver deactivation tickets; shared account exception list
5.2.9 Backup and recovery
We back up every day, no problem.

According to the "Backup and Recovery Procedure", ERP, file server and AD are backed up incrementally every day and fully every week to a NAS, and copied every week to immutable off-site storage. RPO, RTO and the recovery sequence (AD → ERP → file server) are defined for each service. Every quarter, one service is selected for a restore test, and the results and improvements are recorded.
ISMS-I-009 Backup and Recovery Procedure; screenshot of backup schedule; restore test records 2026 Q1–Q3
8.2.5 Access control for the prototype area
The prototype area has access control.

The prototype area (Building B, 2nd floor) uses electronic access control. Access is requested by the project manager and approved by the prototype protection officer; the system shows the authorized list and access logs. The authorized list is reviewed every quarter, and lost cards are blocked immediately according to the procedure.
PP-P-003 Prototype Area Access Control Procedure; access authorization list; access right review record 2026 Q3; card blocking records

blocks.title: The golden rule of the self-assessment
blocks.text: Write what you really do, and prove what you write. The self-assessment is the script for assessment day: the auditor will ask for evidence sentence by sentence based on what you wrote.

summary: Implementation roadmap: gap analysis → scope → risk assessment → documents → implementation → internal audit → management review → ISA self-assessment → formal assessment.
Timelines vary greatly with your starting point and objectives. Maturity level 3 needs evidence that processes run continuously, so let each process run through at least one full cycle.
The document list should map to every ISA control and show approval, version and operating records.
Information security is cross-departmental work. The RACI table must include HR, facilities, purchasing, R&D and other roles.

In the ISA self-assessment, the implementation description must address the Must, Should, high and very high requirements specifically, and the reference documentation must give document numbers and record names that can be requested.

chapters.title: TISAX Audit Practice (2) — Assessment Day and Auditee Skills
chapters.title_en: TISAX Audit Practice (2): Assessment Day and Auditee Skills
intro: Assessment day is when you "show" the work of the past months. With the same management system, a prepared team answers clearly and in a structured way and shows evidence quickly. An unprepared team may make one guessed answer that leads the auditor to dig much deeper.

This chapter covers the opening meeting, interview skills, the AL3 site tour route, sampling, remote assessment tips and the auditor's decision logic, so you know what the auditor across the table is thinking.

blocks.text: 1. Final preparation before the assessment

items: Confirm the assessment agenda: which controls and interviewees are planned for each time slot, and ask interviewees to block the time.
Prepare evidence folders: create a folder for each control number (for example 1.1.1, 4.1.3) with the latest version of documents and records, so you can open them quickly during the assessment.
Prepare the meeting room and equipment: projector, network, a computer that can share its screen. For AL3, arrange escorts and access rights for the site tour.
Appoint an "evidence coordinator": this person pulls up documents in real time during interviews, so the interviewees can focus on answering.
Run mock interviews with the interviewees, using the Possible questions of each control.

blocks.text: 2. Opening meeting

items: Introductions: the auditor, the management representative of the audited organization, the ISMS manager and the contact persons of each department.
Confirm the assessment scope, assessment objectives, assessment level and sites.
Confirm the agenda, interviewees, site tour route and breaks.
Explain the assessment method (document review, interviews, on-site observation, sampling), how findings are classified, and the next steps.
Confirm rules for confidentiality, photography and network use (the audited organization's security rules also apply to the auditor).
Top management gives a short company overview and states its commitment to information security, showing management support.

blocks.text: Please make sure the managing director or plant manager attends the opening meeting, even if only for ten minutes. When the auditor hears top management explain the security objectives in person, it makes a real difference to their impression of management commitment under 1.2.1.
3. Interview skills: how auditees should answer

head: Principle
Explanation
Example
rows: Listen carefully before answering
If you are unsure about the question, ask the auditor to repeat or rephrase it.
"Do you want to know about the account request process, or how often accounts are reviewed?"
Answer the question itself, do not expand
Stop when you have answered. Do not move into areas you were not asked about.
Asked "How often are access rights reviewed?", answer "Every six months, the last one was in June", then show the record.
Do not guess
If you do not know, say so, and say who would know or where to find out.
"IT is responsible for this. I will ask the IT manager to explain."
Show evidence
After you speak, show the evidence. Words alone prove nothing.
"This is the account review report for the first half of 2026. It contains the review results for 12 systems."
Describe what you actually do
Explain how you really do it. Do not recite the documents.
The auditor would rather see how you work than hear you read the procedure aloud.
Admit gaps and explain improvements
If there is a gap, admit it honestly and explain the known improvement plan.
"This is only 80% complete at the moment. The rest is planned for completion by the end of November; here is the project plan."
Stay consistent
Different interviewees must describe the same process in the same way, so align everyone in daily work.
If HR says accounts are disabled on the leaving day but IT says it is done the following week, the auditor will dig deeper.

blocks.title: Things you must never do
blocks.text: Do not guess, do not make things up, do not create records at the last minute with back-dated dates, and do not blame each other in front of the auditor. If a last-minute fake record is discovered (for example, the file was created the day before the assessment), it seriously damages the auditor's trust in the whole ISMS.
4. Site tour (AL3): key route

head: Stop
What auditors often look at
Related controls
rows: Main gate and security desk
Visitor registration, confidentiality commitment, visitor badges, escort rules, posted photography rules
Office area
Clear desk, screen lock, classification labels on documents, documents left at printers, whiteboard content
Server room / network equipment room
Access control and access logs, locked racks, UPS and environmental monitoring, cable labeling, unrelated items
Delivery and shipping area
Whether the delivery and shipping area is included in the zone concept, handover records for parcels and prototypes
Prototype area
Fence or perimeter, strength of the building shell, window screening, type of access control, intrusion detection, separation between customers, photography control
Production line and OT
Accounts on production PCs, USB control, anti-malware or compensating measures, network segmentation
Meeting rooms and shared spaces
Video conference equipment, documents left behind, sound and visual protection (high protection needs)
Media disposal and recycling area
Shredder security level, disposal records, safekeeping of media waiting for disposal

blocks.text: Walk the tour route in advance, ideally with an auditor's eyes: are there drawings in the waste bins, have the meeting room whiteboards been wiped, can you see into the prototype area windows from outside? Once, I saw the roller door of a prototype area half open while I was still in the parking lot.
5. Sampling

items: Auditors usually take samples from a population. For example: pick a few leavers from the leaver list and check the account deactivation dates; pick a few change requests and check approval and test records; pick a few new hires and check confidentiality commitments and training records.

Sampling often uses "cross-checking": leaving dates in the HR system against AD account deactivation times; the access authorization list against the current employee list; the asset inventory against equipment on site.
The sampling period usually covers a past period of time, to confirm that processes run continuously (this relates to maturity level 3).
Have complete population lists ready (for example, all leavers and all change requests of the past year), so the auditor can select samples on the spot.
If the sample shows exceptions, the auditor may extend the sample to decide whether it is an isolated case or a systemic problem.

blocks.text: 6. Remote assessment tips

items: Test the video platform, screen sharing and network stability in advance, and prepare a backup option (for example, a spare account or a phone connection).
Provide documents in the way the audit provider requires: screen sharing or secure upload. For highly confidential documents, prefer screen sharing only and do not send files.
Show system settings "live" (for example, log in to Entra ID to show the MFA policy, or show coverage in the EDR console). This is more convincing than screenshots.
Interviewees should be in a quiet, undisturbed room where the background shows no sensitive information. Test the camera and microphone in advance.
Pay attention to the security of the remote assessment itself: do not share the meeting link outside the group, and close unrelated windows and notifications before sharing your screen.

blocks.text: 7. Decision logic from the auditor's perspective

head: Question
What the auditor thinks
What the auditee should prepare
rows: Is the objective achieved?
First look at the Objective: has the purpose of this control been achieved?
Be able to explain in one sentence how the control objective is achieved.
Are all Must requirements met?
Must requirements are strict, with no exceptions. Missing one usually means a non-conformity.
Evidence mapped to each Must requirement.
Are deviations from Should requirements justified?
A Should requirement that is not implemented needs a valid reason; the organization understands the impact and explains it reasonably. Without a reason, it counts as a finding.
A deviation list: reason, impact assessment, approver.
Do high / very high requirements apply, and are they met?
Check the additional requirements marked C, I, A according to the assessment objectives.
List the applicable additional requirements and evidence according to the assessment objectives.
Is there a decision for every aspect?
Every aspect listed under "The following aspects are considered" should have a well-considered decision and reason.
A small table: aspect, decision, reason, evidence.
Is maturity level 3 reached?
The auditor needs to see "standardization (documented, integrated into the overall system, clear roles) plus evidence of continuous operation (records over a period, multiple executions)".
Records across periods, and a description of interfaces between the process and other processes.
Isolated case or systemic?
A single exception may be a minor non-conformity or an observation; repeated or widespread gaps may be rated as a major non-conformity.
The complete population and an explanation of the root cause.

blocks.title: What evidence for maturity level 3 looks like
blocks.text: Take account reviews as an example: an "Account and Access Management Procedure" defines frequency and owner (standardized), the procedure has clear interfaces with the HR leaver process and the change process (integrated), and there are review reports and follow-up records for several consecutive periods (continuous operation). A procedure without records is level 2 or lower; records for only one period make it hard to prove continuous operation.
I see! The auditor is not trying to make trouble, but uses a fixed logic: objective, Must, Should, high and very high, aspects, maturity, systemic. We just prepare in that order.

summary: Before the assessment: agenda and interviewees, evidence folders by control number, an evidence coordinator, mock interviews.
Ask top management to attend the opening meeting; confirm scope, objectives, level, agenda and rules.
Interview principles: listen carefully, answer only what is asked, do not guess, show evidence, describe what you actually do, admit gaps, stay consistent.
Key AL3 tour stops: main gate and visitors, office area, server room, delivery and shipping area, prototype area, production OT, meeting rooms, disposal area.
Sampling often cross-checks data from different systems and covers a period of time to confirm continuous operation.
For remote assessments, test the platform, show system settings live, and protect the security of the assessment itself.
Decision logic: one missing Must means a non-conformity; Should deviations need a reasonable justification; maturity level 3 needs standardization plus evidence of continuous operation.

chapters.title: TISAX Audit Practice (3) — Top 30 Findings and Corrective Actions
chapters.title_en: TISAX Audit Practice (3): Top 30 Findings and Corrective Actions
intro: This chapter lists the 30 most common types of findings from consulting and audit practice, mapped to ISA 2027.1 control numbers, with suggested corrective actions. You can use this table as a self-check list before your assessment.

After you receive findings, the key is to write a corrective action plan (CAP) that convinces the auditor: not just fixing the one record in front of you, but finding the root cause, preventing recurrence and proving that the measures work. At the end of this chapter we explain how to write a CAP and how to prepare for the follow-up assessment.

blocks.text: 1. Top 30 common findings

These are common "types" of findings. Whether a case is really a non-conformity, and how serious it is, depends on the auditor's overall judgment of objective achievement, Must and Should requirements and protection needs.

head: No. / Control
Finding (auditor's view)
Suggested correction
rows: The security policy is approved, but employees cannot get the latest version through the intranet or another channel; or policy changes were not communicated to external partners.
Publish the policy on the intranet and set up a change notification process (employees and external partners); keep notification records.
The ISMS scope does not match the TISAX assessment scope, or there is no evidence that management reviews ISMS effectiveness regularly.
Update the ISMS scope document and map it to the assessment scope; set up an annual management review and keep records.
The information security officer has many other roles, with no defined authority or resources; customers do not know the external contact point.
Formally appoint the officer and define authority, responsibilities and resources; update the security contact in contracts or customer portals.
The asset inventory lists only hardware; information assets, their supporting assets and owners are not identified.
Rebuild the inventory around information assets, map supporting assets and owners, and review it regularly.
A classification scheme exists, but handling rules for transfer, storage and disposal per level are not defined, or labeling is not applied.
Add handling rules per classification level and communicate them; spot-check document labels and M365 sensitivity label settings.
Employees use unassessed cloud services or AI tools to process customer data on their own; there is no approved list.
Set up an assessment and approval process and list for external IT services, block unapproved services technically, and check usage regularly.
There is no software approval procedure, users can install software themselves, and maintenance tools are not included in approval.
Create an approved software list and request process, remove local administrator rights, include maintenance tools and review regularly.
The risk assessment has not been updated for three years, risks have no risk owner, and treatment plans have no progress tracking.
Reassess periodically and when events occur, as defined in the procedure; assign risk owners; set up a treatment plan tracking sheet.
Internal audits cover only ISO clauses, not ISA controls; non-conformities are not tracked to closure.
Plan internal audit scope and schedule based on the ISA; set up non-conformity tracking and effectiveness checks.
No independent review is performed; the ISMS manager audits the processes they are responsible for.
Have an independent and competent auditor or external body perform the review, and report results to management.
Employees do not know what a reportable security event is, and external parties have no reporting channel.
Define reportable events and communicate them; set up internal and external reporting channels (mailbox, hotline) and publish them on the website and in contracts.
Incident handling has no categorization or prioritization; response times and escalation are not defined (high protection needs).
Define incident categories and classification, response times, escalation paths and communication strategy; keep handling and lessons-learned records.
There is no crisis management plan, or the members and authority of the crisis team are not defined.
Create a crisis management plan with team members, activation criteria and communication strategy, and run a tabletop exercise.
Temporary or contractor staff have not signed confidentiality and security policy compliance commitments.
Require staff from staffing agencies and contractors to sign commitments, or agree on this in the contract and obtain the staff list.
Training is only for new hires; there is no annual training plan for target groups (such as top management, administrators, production staff).
Set up a training concept and annual plan including target groups and top management training; track completion rates.
There are no rules for home office and business travel; shared office spaces, privacy screens in public places and theft protection are not considered.
Create mobile working rules covering private and public environments, information handling, theft protection and secure access, and communicate them.
The security zone concept does not cover the delivery and shipping area, and employees do not know the rules of conduct for each zone.
Update the zone map and protection measures, include the delivery and shipping area, and publish and communicate the rules of conduct.
Scrapped hard disks are handed to a recycler without proof of destruction; for high protection needs, disposal does not follow a standard.
Set up a media disposal procedure, dispose per a standard such as ISO 21964 (at least security level 4 for high protection needs) and obtain certificates.
Not all laptops are encrypted, and USB flash drives can be used freely.
Enforce encryption with BitLocker and MDM and produce reports; control and register removable storage media.
There are no issue and return records for access cards and tokens, and no blocking procedure when they are lost.
Keep lifecycle records for identification means (production, handover, return, destruction, loss handling).
External services (VPN, webmail) do not use strong authentication based on a risk assessment, and privileged accounts do not use MFA.
Introduce MFA or PAM for externally accessible services and privileged accounts based on a risk assessment.
Leavers' accounts are disabled only weeks later, there are uncontrolled shared accounts, and accounts are not reviewed regularly.
Link to the HR leaver process to disable accounts immediately, register shared account exceptions, and set up periodic account reviews (incl. customer systems).
Access right reviews do not cover privileged and technical accounts or rights in customer systems; rights are not adjusted when people change jobs.
Define a review scope list and cycle including privileged and technical accounts and customer systems, and link it to the job change process.
Confidential customer drawings are sent unencrypted as normal e-mail attachments.
Use encrypted transfer or a secure file exchange platform according to the classification rules; communicate this and support it with DLP.
Logs are not stored centrally, nobody reviews them regularly, and administrator activities are not logged.
Assess which systems must be logged, collect and protect logs centrally, and define periodic review and escalation of anomalies.
There is no process to collect and assess vulnerability information, patching has no deadlines and is not verified, and OT systems have not been updated for a long time without compensating measures.
Set up a vulnerability management procedure (sources, CVSS, deadlines, verification); handle OT risks with compensating measures such as segmentation.
Office, production OT and guest networks are not segmented, and management interfaces of network devices can be reached from normal network segments.
Segment networks and set firewall rules based on risk, restrict access to management interfaces, and keep a network diagram.
Backups exist but restores have never been tested; backups are in the same domain as production and could be encrypted by ransomware.
Define a backup and recovery concept (incl. RPO and RTO), test restores regularly, and set up offline or immutable backups.
Suppliers have not had a security risk assessment and contracts have no security clauses; drawings were handed over before an NDA was signed, or the NDA has expired.
Set up supplier security assessments and contract clause templates; confirm a valid NDA before disclosure and track validity.
For prototype projects, the customer's classification, camouflage and transport requirements were not obtained; the prototype area windows can be seen into from outside.
Keep a list of customer requirements per order and communicate it; use film, blinds or partitions for visual screening and inspect regularly.

blocks.text: Of these 30, the three I see most often on site are: leavers' accounts not disabled immediately (4.1.3), backups never restore-tested (5.2.9), and employees using unapproved cloud or AI tools (1.3.3). Check these three first before your assessment.
2. How to write a corrective action plan (CAP)

items: **Finding description**: quote the auditor's finding and the control number in full. Do not rewrite or soften it.
**Impact assessment**: check whether the same problem also exists in other systems, departments or sites (horizontal deployment).
**Root cause analysis**: use "five whys" or a fishbone diagram to find the root causes in processes, rules, tools or competence. Do not stop at "human error".
**Correction (immediate action)**: fix the immediate problem first, for example disable the account or get the missing NDA signed.

**Corrective action (prevent recurrence)**: address the root cause by revising the process, introducing tools or automation, or improving training, and explain how this prevents the same problem from happening again.
**Owner and deadline**: each measure needs a named owner and a realistic completion date. Deadlines must fit the timelines set by the audit provider and ENX.
**Effectiveness check**: define how you will prove the measure works, for example records over several periods, internal audit sample results or KPIs.

head: CAP field
Example
rows: Finding description
4.1.3: Of 5 sampled leavers, the AD accounts of 2 were disabled only 10 and 23 days after they left.
Impact assessment
All 38 leavers of the past 12 months were checked; 9 were disabled late. No abnormal logins during the delay periods were confirmed.
Root cause analysis
The HR leaver process did not formally notify IT (only verbal notice), IT compared lists only once a month in a batch, and the procedure did not define a deadline for disabling accounts.
Correction (immediate action)
All leavers' accounts have been disabled; login records during the delay periods have been checked (report attached).
Corrective action (prevent recurrence)

Revise the "Account and Access Management Procedure" to require disabling on the last working day; submitting the HR leaver form automatically creates an IT ticket; weekly automatic comparison of the HR list with AD accounts.
Owner
IT manager (process and system), HR manager (leaver form process)
Deadline
Procedure revision: 2026-11-15; system integration: 2026-12-15
Effectiveness check
Weekly comparison reports with zero differences for 3 consecutive months; in the 2027-03 internal audit, 100% of sampled leavers disabled on their last working day.

blocks.title: CAPs that often get rejected
blocks.text: Root cause written as "human error", measures limited to "more awareness", no deadline or owner, no way to check effectiveness, or only the sampled case is fixed without checking for the same problem elsewhere.
3. Follow-up assessment

items: The audit provider decides how to follow up depending on the type of finding: document review (you submit evidence), remote interview, or an on-site check (for example, for physical security improvements).

When you prepare evidence, provide it for each CAP measure: revised documents (with version and approval), system setting screens, records after implementation (ideally over a period of time), and internal audit or self-check results.

Major non-conformities usually must be confirmed as corrected in a follow-up assessment before the full label is issued. For minor non-conformities, once the CAP is accepted, a temporary label is usually issued first, and corrections must be completed within the deadline.

Deadlines for each stage (for example, CAP submission, completion of corrections, follow-up assessment) are set by the audit provider and the latest ENX Participant Handbook. Build a countdown schedule as soon as you receive the report.
Observations and room for improvement do not affect the label, but add them to next year's improvement plan so they do not become non-conformities at the reassessment.

blocks.text: Taking notes! The five treasures of a CAP: root cause, measures, owner, deadline, effectiveness check. Miss one and it may be rejected.

The best CAP I have ever seen automated the leaver deactivation for 4.1.3 and attached three months of weekly comparison reports. The auditor closed it in five minutes. Corrective actions are not written for the auditor; they are there so the same problem never happens again.

summary: The Top 30 common findings work as a self-check list before the assessment. The most common are leaver account deactivation, restore tests, and unapproved cloud or AI tools.
A CAP must include the finding description, impact assessment, root cause analysis, immediate correction, measures to prevent recurrence, owner, deadline and effectiveness check.
Do not stop the root cause at "human error", and do not limit measures to "more awareness".
Follow-up assessments are by document review, remote or on site, depending on the finding. Major non-conformities must be confirmed as corrected before the full label is issued.
Deadlines follow the audit provider and the latest ENX rules. Build a countdown schedule as soon as you receive the report.

lines.text: Welcome to the audit practice module! We have read the controls one by one. Now we turn them into a real project you can actually run!

slide.title: Audit Practice 1: Preparation and Planning
bullets: The nine phases of the roadmap
How to estimate a typical timeline

lines.text: Right. Understanding the controls is only step one. Many companies get stuck not because they do not understand the controls, but because they do not know where to start or how long it will take.
So Allan, if the boss says tomorrow that we are doing TISAX, what is the very first thing to do?
First, ask the customer which label they need. Second, do a gap analysis. Do not start by writing documents with your head down.

In a gap analysis, you take the original ISA 2027.1 text, go through it question by question in interviews, look at evidence, and mark the current maturity and gaps. The result is a list of improvement projects.
I have one habit in gap analysis. I always look at the evidence, not just listen to explanations. Very often people say they have it, and then you open the folder and it is empty.
Ha ha, the folder name is perfect, and there is nothing inside.
Step two is defining the scope. Decide which sites, organizations and processes are in the assessment, confirm the assessment objectives and level, and then register with ENX.
Step three is risk assessment. Build the asset inventory and classification, identify risks, assign risk owners and set up treatment plans. That covers 1.3.1, 1.3.2 and 1.4.1.
Step four is writing documents, filling the gaps with policies, procedures and forms. Step five is implementation: MFA, EDR, backup, access control, training, and you start building up records.
Step six is the internal audit, checking question by question against the ISA. Step seven is the management review. Step eight is the ISA self-assessment. Only step nine is the formal assessment.
Wow, nine steps! So how long does it take in total?

slide.title: Typical Timelines, for Reference Only
bullets: Not an ENX rule, depends on your case

lines.text: That is the hardest question, because every company starts from a different place. I can only share the common ranges from my consulting experience. They are not ENX rules.
If you already have ISO 27001 and it has been running for more than a year, it usually takes about 3 to 6 months. You mainly add the ISA-specific requirements and evidence.
If you have basic IT management but no ISMS, it is about 6 to 12 months, because you need to build the framework and let the processes run for a while.
If you add Prototype Protection, it often takes another 2 to 6 months, because fences, access control, intrusion detection and window screening all need construction and purchasing.
One of my clients waited three months just for the delivery of a new access control system for the prototype area. So please start physical improvements first.
So can we go to the assessment right after we finish writing the documents? That would be faster.

slide.title: Maturity Level 3 Needs Time
bullets: Standardized process plus evidence it runs
A process released last week rarely gets 3
Run at least one full cycle
For example quarterly reviews, a restore test

lines.text: That is the sentence I fear most. The assessment is next month, so we will finish writing the documents this month.
Maturity level 3 requires evidence that the process has been used continuously and actively over a longer period. Finished documents are only the start of maturity level 2.

In practice, I recommend letting a new process run through at least one full cycle before the assessment. For example one quarter of account reviews, one restore test, one internal audit and one management review.
I often tell clients that TISAX is like making pickles. Even with a great recipe, you have to give it time before the flavor develops.
Ha ha, so we need pickling time! Are there any tips for planning the schedule?

Plan backwards. Confirm the assessment date with the audit provider. Count back two months for self-assessment, internal audit and management review, then three months for running processes. The rest is your build phase.
Also, put long lead time items like physical improvements and system purchases at the very beginning. Documents can be written in parallel.
Taking notes! Ask the customer first, do a gap analysis first, start physical improvements early, and let each process run at least one cycle.
In the next part, we look at the document list, RACI roles, and good and bad ways to fill in the self-assessment!

video.title: Document List, RACI and Writing the ISA Self-Assessment

lines.text: This part is very practical! We will look at the document list, roles and responsibilities, and the self-assessment that gives everyone a headache.

slide.title: Key Points of This Part
bullets: Document list mapped to ISA controls

lines.text: Let us start with documents. The handout has a list of more than 40 documents, each mapped to ISA controls. You can use it directly for your inventory.
Let me pick a few that are often missed. First, assessment and approval records for external IT services, control 1.3.3. Today even AI tools count.
The ISA definition of cloud or external IT services even lists AI chatbots and AI agents as examples. If an employee puts a customer drawing into an AI translator, that is this control.
Wow, I think someone in our sales team put a specification into an AI tool yesterday to summarize it.
That is exactly why you need an approved list. The second one often missed is the approved software list, control 1.3.4, and maintenance tools must be included too.
The third is records for identification means, control 4.1.1. Production, return and loss handling of access cards, tokens and keys. Many companies have just one spreadsheet, and it is out of date.
The fourth is restore test records, control 5.2.9. Having backups is nothing special. Having restore test records is what counts.
Do we need to write lots of documents? Our company has only three IT people.
You do not need many documents, and you can merge them. Four things matter. Easy to find, the latest version, approved by someone, and records that prove they are really used.
Next is the RACI table. What do R, A, C and I stand for?
R is responsible, the one who does the work. A is accountable, the final owner. C is the people you consult, and I is the people you inform. Each activity can have only one A.
The most common problem I see is a table where IT is A for everything. Information security is not just an IT topic!

Personnel screening and confidentiality commitments belong to HR. Access control and visitors belong to facilities. Suppliers and NDAs belong to purchasing and legal. Prototypes are R&D and facilities together.
In interviews, the auditor goes straight to these departments. If the HR manager says security is an IT thing, it will be very hard to get a 3 on that control.
So true. I think I have heard that sentence at some company before.
Finally, the self-assessment! How do we write the Implementation description and the Reference documentation?

slide.title: Writing the Implementation Description
bullets: Who, does what, with which tool
How often, which records are kept
Respond to each Must and Should
Give reasons for Should not done

lines.text: Here is a formula for the implementation description. Who does what, with which tool, how often, and which records are kept. Then respond to each Must and Should one by one.
Take 4.1.3 as an example. A weak answer is, IT manages accounts and deletes them when people leave. The auditor will ask ten follow-up questions about that sentence.
A good answer is, account changes are handled by ticket according to the procedure, the HR leaver form creates a ticket the same day, and IT disables the AD and M365 accounts on the last working day.

Then add that shared accounts exist only for two production HMI stations, approved and recorded in the exception list, and that account reviews happen every six months, including customer portal accounts.
Wow, what a difference! The good answer already answers the questions the auditor wanted to ask.
Reference documentation is the same. Do not write see ISMS documents. Write the document number, title and version, plus the record names, so the auditor can request them directly.

slide.title: Writing the Reference Documentation
bullets: Avoid writing only see ISMS documents

lines.text: And be honest about maturity. If you rate everything a 3 but the evidence cannot support it, the auditor loses trust in the whole self-assessment and asks more detailed questions on every control after that.
On the other hand, if you rate yourself conservatively but the evidence is strong, the auditor will usually rate based on the evidence. Honesty is the best strategy.
And for a Should requirement we do not implement, what do we write in the self-assessment?
State the reason for not doing it, the impact assessment and who approved it. Do not leave it blank. And for every item under The following aspects are considered, write your decision and the reason.

Taking notes! Documents easy to find, approved and with records, do not make IT the A for everything, use the formula for implementation descriptions, give document numbers, and rate maturity honestly.
The self-assessment is the script for assessment day. Write what you really do, and prove what you write.
In the next part we go into assessment day! The opening meeting and interview skills, and Allan will share what auditors really think!

video.title: Final Preparation, Opening Meeting and Interview Skills

lines.text: Finally, assessment day! Honestly, just thinking about being interviewed by an auditor makes me nervous.
Do not be nervous. Auditors are human too. When I sit across the table, I actually hope the auditee does well, because that makes my job easier as well.

There are a few things you must get right before the assessment. First, confirm the agenda: which controls are covered in each time slot and who is interviewed. Tell people early so they can block the time.

slide.title: Final Preparation
bullets: Run a round of mock interviews

lines.text: Second, prepare evidence folders. Create a folder for each control number, for example 1.1.1 or 4.1.3, with the latest documents and records.
Third, appoint an evidence coordinator. The interviewee focuses on answering, and the coordinator pulls up the documents in real time.
This trick works really well. In the smoothest assessment I have seen, by the time the auditor finished the question, the record was already on the screen. The whole day had a great rhythm.
Fourth, run a round of mock interviews using the Possible questions of each control. It is better to be stumped by a colleague than by the auditor on assessment day.
And what happens in the opening meeting at the start of the assessment?
The opening meeting starts with introductions on both sides. Then you confirm the assessment scope, objectives, level and sites, and then the agenda, interviewees and site tour route.
The auditor explains the assessment methods, such as document review, interviews, on-site observation and sampling, plus how findings are classified and what happens next.
Also confirm the rules for confidentiality and photography. Your company's security rules apply to the auditor too, and you can say that openly.
I strongly recommend that the managing director or plant manager attends the opening, even for just ten minutes, to explain the company's security objectives and commitment.
Is it really that important for top management to attend the opening?
Very important. Control 1.2.1 requires management to commission and approve the ISMS and to review its effectiveness regularly. The boss saying it in person is more convincing than any document.
Now the main event, interview skills! What should interviewees pay attention to?

slide.title: How Interviewees Should Answer
bullets: If you do not know, say so

lines.text: First, listen carefully before you answer. If you do not understand, ask the auditor to repeat, or check whether they are asking about the process or the frequency.
Second, answer the question itself and do not expand. If you are asked how often access rights are reviewed, say every six months, the last one was in June, and then show the record.
I once met a very enthusiastic section manager. I only asked about the account review frequency, and he also told me about an old server nobody was looking after. So I had to write it down.
Ha ha, he basically handed the auditor a new question himself!
Third, and most important, do not guess. If you do not know, say you do not know, and then say who would know or where to look.
A wrong guess is worse than I do not know. The auditor will follow your answer, then find that your story does not match the records, and it becomes a bigger problem.
Fourth, show evidence after you answer, because words alone prove nothing. Fifth, describe what you actually do. Do not recite the procedure. The auditor wants to see how you work.
And what if we are asked about something we really have not done well?

slide.title: Admit Gaps and Stay Consistent
bullets: Interviewees must tell the same story

lines.text: Admit it honestly, then explain the improvement plan. For example, this part is eighty percent done, the rest is planned for the end of the month, and here is the project plan.
Also, keep your stories consistent. If HR says accounts are disabled on the leaving day and IT says it is done the next week, the auditor will definitely dig all the way down.

One last warning. Never create records at the last minute or change dates. I once saw a record whose file was created the day before the assessment. At that moment, all trust for the whole day was gone.
That is scary. Honesty really is the best strategy.
And do not blame each other in front of the auditor. Teamwork is part of maturity too, and auditors can always tell.
Taking notes! Evidence folders, an evidence coordinator, the boss at the opening, listen carefully, do not expand, do not guess, show evidence, and tell the same story.
In the next part, we follow the auditor on the site tour, and look at sampling, remote assessments and the decision logic!

video.title: Site Tour, Sampling, Remote Assessment and Decision Logic

lines.text: In this part we take a walk around the site with Allan! What does an AL3 auditor actually look at?
I usually start at the main gate. I look at visitor registration, whether there is a confidentiality commitment, visitor badges, escort rules, and whether the photography rules are posted.

slide.title: Tour Route, Part 1
bullets: Main gate: visitor and photo rules

lines.text: In the office area, I look at clear desks, screen locks, document labels, documents left at the printer, and whether the meeting room whiteboards have been wiped.
In the server room, I look at access control and access logs, whether racks are locked, the UPS and environmental monitoring, and whether the server room has turned into a storage room.
I really once saw a server room full of raffle prizes for the company year-end party, plus a treadmill. The section manager said it was only temporary. It had been temporary for two years.
Ha ha, a server room, storage room and gym all in one. So many functions!
Many companies forget the delivery and shipping area. A Must requirement in 3.1.1 clearly says the security zone concept must consider delivery and shipping areas.

The prototype area is the most important stop. I look at the perimeter, the strength of the building shell, window screening, the type of access control, intrusion detection, customer separation and photo control.
On the production line and OT, I look at workstation accounts, USB control, anti-malware or compensating measures, and whether the network is separated from the office network.
My advice is to walk the route with an auditor's eyes before the assessment. Once, I saw the roller door of a prototype area half open from the parking lot, before I even reached the main gate.
Wow, a finding before even entering the company gate!
So how do auditors take samples?

slide.title: Sampling and Cross-Checking
bullets: Sample from a population, such as leavers
Cover a period to see continuous operation
Exceptions may lead to a larger sample

lines.text: The auditor samples from a population. For example, they pick a few people from the leaver list and check account deactivation dates, or pick a few change requests and check approval and test records.
And they cross-check. Leaving dates in the HR system against AD deactivation times, the access authorization list against current employees, and the asset inventory against equipment on site.
Samples cover a past period of time to confirm the process runs continuously. That is exactly how they check maturity level 3.

Please have the complete population ready, like all leavers and all change requests of the past year, so the auditor can select samples on the spot. If they find an exception, they may take a bigger sample.
Many assessments are remote now. What should we watch out for?

slide.title: Remote Assessment Tips
bullets: Test the platform and have a backup
Share sensitive documents on screen only

lines.text: First, test the video platform, screen sharing and network in advance, and prepare a backup option, like a spare account or a phone connection.
Second, show system settings live. For example, log in to Entra ID to show the MFA policy, or open the EDR console to show coverage. That is more convincing than screenshots.
Third, share sensitive documents on screen, you do not always need to send files. Fourth, close unrelated windows and notifications before you share your screen.
Once, during screen sharing, a chat message from a colleague popped up in the corner saying, careful, this auditor asks very detailed questions. Everyone burst out laughing.
Finally, how does the auditor actually decide?
This is the order in my head. First, is the Objective achieved? Then, are all Must requirements met? Missing even one Must usually means a non-conformity.
Next comes Should. For anything not done, is there a valid reason, an impact assessment and an approval? A deviation without a reason is still a finding.
Then I look at the high and very high requirements according to the assessment objectives, and check that each item under The following aspects are considered has a well-considered decision.
Last, I judge the maturity level. For a 3, I need to see standardization, meaning documented, integrated into the overall system and with clear roles, plus evidence of continuous operation.
Take account reviews. There is a procedure defining frequency and owner, an interface with the HR leaver process, and reports for several consecutive periods. That is a 3.
I also decide whether it is an isolated case or systemic. A single exception may be a minor non-conformity or an observation. The same problem everywhere may be a major non-conformity.
I see! Objective, Must, Should, high and very high, aspects, maturity, systemic. If we prepare in that order, we are on the right track!
In the next part, Allan reveals the 30 findings he writes most often! Get your notebooks ready!
Here it is, what everyone has been waiting for! The Top 30 common findings! Allan, which ones do you write most often on site?

slide.title: Audit Practice 3: Common Findings
bullets: A self-check list before the assessment

lines.text: This table is the result of many years of consulting and auditing, with plenty of painful lessons. The handout has all 30. Here I will pick the highlights, and you can use them for a self-check.

Let us start with the top three. Number one is 4.1.3, leavers' accounts not disabled immediately. The Must requirement is very clear: disable them immediately after the person leaves the organization.

slide.title: The Top Three
bullets: 4.1.3 Leaver accounts not disabled in time

lines.text: The typical case is that HR tells IT verbally, IT processes it in a monthly batch, and the account is still active two or three weeks after the person has left.
Number two is 5.2.9. Backups exist but restores have never been tested, and the backups sit in the same domain as production. When ransomware hits, everything gets encrypted.
Number three is 1.3.3. Employees use unassessed cloud services or AI tools to process customer data, and the company has no approved list.
Number three feels very modern. AI tools made the list too!
So what are the common findings in the policies and organization chapter?

slide.title: Common Findings in Chapter 1
bullets: 1.1.1 Staff cannot get the latest policy

lines.text: For 1.1.1, the policy is approved, but employees cannot find the latest version on the intranet, or changes were not sent to external partners. Note that making policies available to employees became a Must in 2027.
For 1.3.1, the asset inventory lists only computers and servers. The information assets themselves are not identified, and there are no owners.
For 1.3.4, there is no software approval. Everyone is a local administrator and installs whatever they like, and nobody controls the maintenance tools at all.
For 1.4.1, the risk assessment has not been updated for three years, risks have no risk owner, and the treatment plans have no progress tracking.
For 1.5.2, there is no independent review. The ISMS manager audits the processes they are responsible for, and that does not meet the independence requirement.
For 1.6.1, employees do not know what a reportable security event is, and external parties have no reporting channel. For 1.6.3, there is no crisis management plan.
And what about the HR and physical security chapters?

slide.title: Common Findings in Chapters 2 and 3
bullets: 2.1.2 Temp staff did not sign commitments
2.1.3 Only new-hire training, none for leaders
3.1.3 No proof of hard disk destruction

lines.text: For 2.1.2, temporary or contractor staff did not sign confidentiality and security policy commitments. For 2.1.3, there is only new-hire training, with no annual plan and nothing for top management.
For 2.1.4, there are no rules for home office and business travel, and nobody has thought about shared offices, privacy in public places or theft protection.
For 3.1.3, scrapped hard disks go to a recycler with no proof of destruction. For high protection needs, disposal must follow a standard such as ISO 21964, at least security level 4.
For 3.1.4, not all laptops are encrypted and anyone can plug in a USB stick. You can solve this nicely with BitLocker plus MDM reports.
Identity and access and IT security must be the big problem areas, right?
Yes, these two chapters have a lot. For 4.1.1, there are no issue and return records for access cards and tokens, and nobody knows how to block them when they are lost.
For 4.1.2, external services such as VPN and webmail do not use MFA based on risk, and privileged accounts have no stronger authentication.
For 4.2.1, the access review covers only normal accounts and misses privileged accounts, technical accounts and rights inside customer systems.
For 5.2.4, logs are not stored centrally and nobody reviews them. For 5.2.5, nobody collects vulnerability information, and OT systems have not been updated for years with no compensating measures.
For 5.2.7, the office network, production OT and guest network are all in one segment, and any normal PC can reach the management interfaces of network devices.
Finally, suppliers and prototypes. What is common there?
For 6.1.1, suppliers had no security risk assessment and contracts have no security clauses. For 6.1.2, drawings were handed over before an NDA was signed, or the NDA expired long ago.
For 8.1.2, the customer's classification, camouflage and transport requirements were not obtained for the prototype project. For 8.2.4, you can see into the prototype area windows from outside.
Use these 30 findings for a self-check before your assessment. Every box you tick is one less surprise on assessment day.
Taking notes! The top three are leaver accounts, restore tests, and unapproved cloud and AI tools. Always check them before the assessment!
In the next part: what do you do after you receive findings? We learn how to write a corrective action plan that gets accepted!

video.title: Corrective Action Plan (CAP) and Follow-Up Assessment

lines.text: The assessment is over and the list of findings has arrived. What now? I think everyone feels discouraged when they first see the report.
Findings are normal. I rarely see a company with zero findings in its first assessment. What matters is the next step, the corrective action plan, or CAP.
A CAP has several required fields. First, the finding description. Quote the auditor's wording and the control number in full. Do not rewrite or soften it.
Second, the impact assessment, also called horizontal deployment. Check whether the same problem also exists in other systems, departments or sites.
Third, root cause analysis. Use five whys or a fishbone diagram to find the root causes in processes, rules, tools or competence.
The CAPs I reject most often say the root cause is human error and the measure is more awareness. Written like that, it will definitely happen again.
But sometimes a colleague really did just forget, right?
Then ask why one more time. Why did they forget? Was there no deadline in the process? No reminder? Were the systems not connected? The answer is usually there.
Fourth, the correction, which means fixing the immediate problem, for example disabling the account right away or getting the missing NDA signed.
Fifth, the corrective action. Address the root cause by fixing the process, adding tools or automation, or improving training, so it does not happen again.
Sixth, owner and deadline. Each measure needs a named owner and a realistic completion date. Seventh, the effectiveness check, meaning how you will prove that it works.
Can you give us a complete CAP example?

slide.title: CAP Example for 4.1.3
bullets: Root cause: verbal notice, monthly batch
Measure: leaver form opens an IT ticket

lines.text: Sure, let us use 4.1.3. The finding is that of five sampled leavers, the AD accounts of two were disabled only ten and twenty-three days after they left.
For the wider check, all thirty-eight leavers of the past twelve months were checked. Nine were disabled late, and it was confirmed that there were no abnormal logins during the delay.
The root cause was that the HR leaver process did not formally notify IT. It relied on verbal notice, IT compared lists only once a month, and the procedure had no deadline for disabling accounts.

Immediate correction: disable all leaver accounts and check login records. To prevent recurrence: require disabling on the last working day in the procedure, and let the HR leaver form open an IT ticket automatically.
Add a weekly automatic comparison of the HR list and AD accounts. The owners are the IT manager and the HR manager, each with their own completion date.

The effectiveness check is three consecutive months of weekly reports with zero differences, plus the next internal audit finding one hundred percent of sampled leavers disabled on their last working day.

slide.title: Effectiveness Check
bullets: Three months of reports, zero differences
Measures must prove they really work

lines.text: Wow, written like that, it would be hard for the auditor to say no!
The best CAP I have ever seen was exactly like this, with three months of weekly reports attached. I closed it in five minutes.
And after the CAP is submitted, there is a follow-up assessment, right?

slide.title: Follow-Up Assessment
bullets: Document review, remote or on site
Major findings: verified before full label
Deadlines follow the latest ENX rules

lines.text: Right. The audit provider decides how to follow up depending on the finding. It may be a document review, a remote interview, or a return visit on site, for example for physical security improvements.
When you prepare evidence, match each measure with evidence: revised documents, system setting screens, and records after implementation, ideally over a period of time.

For a major non-conformity, the full label usually comes only after the follow-up assessment confirms it is fixed. For a minor non-conformity, you can usually get a temporary label once the CAP is accepted.
Deadlines for each stage follow the audit provider and the latest ENX Participant Handbook. I recommend building a countdown schedule on the day you receive the report.

Observations and room for improvement do not affect the label, but please add them to next year's improvement plan. Otherwise, at the reassessment three years later, they may well become non-conformities.
Taking notes! The five treasures of a CAP are root cause, measures, owner, deadline and effectiveness check, plus checking for the same problem elsewhere!
Remember, corrective actions are not written for the auditor. They are there so the same problem never happens again.
The next part is the very last one of the course. Allan will sum everything up for us!
Great work, everyone! We have finished the whole ISA 2027 for TISAX course. Allan, please give us a final summary!

slide.title: Course Summary
bullets: TISAX scheme and reading the ISA

lines.text: Thank you all for staying with us this far. We started with what TISAX is, learned to read every field of the ISA, and understood Must, Should and maturity level 3.
Then we went through the Information Security chapters 1 to 7 one by one, plus Prototype Protection and Data Protection, and finally walked through audit practice.
If learners could take away only three sentences, which three would you give them, Allan?

slide.title: Three Sentences to Take Away
bullets: Must has no exceptions, Should needs a reason

lines.text: Sentence one, Must has no exceptions, and Should needs a reason. Sentence two, maturity level 3 means standardized plus continuously in operation.
Sentence three, evidence beats explanations. Write what you really do, and prove what you write.
A TISAX label is usually valid for three years, but security is not a sprint every three years. It is everyday work. Treat it as a management tool, not an exam.
I always say the best assessment is one where the auditor comes and everything is just like a normal day. Although, to be honest, I still rarely see a company like that.
Ha ha, then let us work hard to become that kind of company!
Next, please take the post-course quizzes. Score 80 or more to pass, and you can download your certificate of completion!

slide.title: Next Steps
bullets: Pass mark is 80, get your certificate
Do a gap analysis at your company

lines.text: The quizzes cover the TISAX scheme, reading the ISA, maturity levels and the key points of each chapter. If you are unsure about something, go back to the handout and the chapter summaries.
More importantly, when you go back to your company, do a gap analysis with the original ISA text, and then self-check with the Top 30 findings list.
For details of the assessment rules, keep following the latest ENX Participant Handbook, and always use the latest version of the original ISA text.
ARALE wishes you all a smooth assessment, and the label your customer needs on the first try!
Good luck with your assessments. Maybe we will meet on site during an audit one day. If so, please go easy on me.
Thank you, everyone! See you in the post-course quizzes. Bye bye!
